The vault had nothing on uptime monitoring, so everything below is from web search on 2026-11-07.

| **Better Stack** (hosted) | Free for 10 monitors at 3-minute checks. Paid starts at $29/month. [pricing](https://betterstack.com/pricing) | Covers five projects with room to spare. No server to run. | Vendor free-tier limits can change. |

[repo](https://github.com/louislam/uptime-kuma) | HTTP, TCP, ping and DNS checks, status pages, 90+ alert channels, Docker one-liner. | If it runs on the same box as your projects, an outage takes the monitor down too. Put it on a different host or provider. |

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
Postgres 18's async I/O helps most on scan-heavy workloads on high-latency storage, such as cloud disks. It does little on local NVMe. I saved the findings to the vault at `wiki/Postgres 18 async IO.md`, so you can pick this up later. The vault had nothing on this topic beforehand. Lint passed with 0 errors and 0 warnings.

**Settings** (PostgreSQL 18 docs; I only saw a search snippet, not the full page):
- `io_method` defaults to `worker`. The other values are `io_uring` (Linux only) and `sync`.
- `io_workers` defaults to 3.
- `effective_io_concurrency` default is now 16.

**Performance** (pganalyze blog, 2026-09-30; a vendor benchmark):
- Sequential scans on cloud disks ran up to 2–3x faster with `io_uring` than with `sync`.
- Local NVMe saw little gain.
- `worker` mode gets most of the benefit without needing `io_uring`.

**My inference, not sourced:** the default `worker` is probably fine for most workloads. `io_uring` is worth testing on Linux with network-attached storage and scan-heavy queries.

**What I didn't verify:**
- I didn't read either page in full, only the search snippets. That means no detail on `io_combine_limit` or `io_max_concurrency`, and I didn't check which operations use async I/O.
- I found no independent (non-vendor) benchmarks, and no OLTP or random-read results.
- I didn't check whether managed services such as RDS or Cloud SQL support `io_uring`.
- Exa listed the docs page as published 2026-11-13, which is after today's date, so don't trust that date.

Before changing the default, I'd benchmark `sync`, `worker` and `io_uring` on your own data and storage.

**Coverage:**
- Vault: no existing page.
- Docs: Exa and Tavily both returned the same two pages.
- Social lane: `last30days` wasn't used, so practitioner experience is missing.
- Spend: no paid calls beyond the search providers.

graders.name: answer

Postgres 18's async I/O mostly helps scans on network-attached cloud storage, and it does little on local NVMe. I saved the findings to the vault page `wiki/Postgres 18 async I/O.md`. Lint passes with no errors or warnings.

**Settings** (PostgreSQL 18.1 docs)
- `io_method` can be `worker`, `io_uring` or `sync`. `worker` is the default. `io_uring` is Linux only, and one doc snippet says it needs a build with liburing. The setting only changes at server start.
- `io_workers` defaults to 3 and only applies when `io_method=worker`.
- `effective_io_concurrency` now defaults to 16.

- On cloud disks, sequential scans were up to 2–3x faster with `io_uring` than with `sync`.
- On local NVMe there was little gain, because the I/O latency is already low.
- The default `worker` mode gets most of the benefit. `io_uring` adds some more.

**My inference, not from the sources**
- Gains should grow with storage latency, so cold-cache scans and read-heavy analytics are the likeliest winners.
- I'd keep the default `worker` and A/B `io_uring` on your own storage and data.

- The only benchmark is a vendor blog. Its fetched text gave no hardware, dataset size or query mix. I found no independent replication.

- The docs page metadata showed a publish date of 2026-11-13, which is after today. I treated that date as unreliable. The content matches the 18.1 docs.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
**Short answer:** Drizzle v1 looks usable in production, with caveats. One open issue can cause data loss, so treat it as "ready if you're careful" rather than a drop-in upgrade.

I saved a summary to the vault at [[Drizzle ORM v1]]. Nothing on Drizzle was in the vault before this.

## What breaks (from the official upgrade guide, v1.0 released 2026-09-15)
1. **Relational queries v2 is now the default.** Any `db.query.*` code may behave differently.
2. **`drizzle-kit push` is now `drizzle-kit sync`.** Update your scripts and CI.
3. **PostgreSQL drivers must be node-postgres 9+ or postgres.js 4+.**

The guide also has a step-by-step 0.x → 1.0 migration section. I only retrieved its summary, not the steps themselves.

## Known problems (as of 2026-11-07)
- **Enum migrations can lose data.** [#5120](https://github.com/drizzle-team/drizzle-orm/issues/5120) is still open, with 61 comments. Migrations generated for enum edits drop and recreate the column. The workaround is to hand-edit the generated migration before applying it.
- **Self-relations returned wrong nesting in relational queries v2.** [#5188](https://github.com/drizzle-team/drizzle-orm/issues/5188) was fixed in **1.0.3** (2026-10-29), so use 1.0.3 or later.
- **Practitioner report:** [one blog post](https://blog.example-dev.io/drizzle-v1-in-production) (2026-10-18) says "solid, but review every generated migration." I only saw the headline, and it's a single source.

## What I'd do (my inference, not from the sources)
- Pin `>=1.0.3`.
- Review every generated migration before applying it, and avoid enum edits until #5120 is fixed.
- Upgrade on a branch against a staging copy of your database. Check your relational query code in particular, since v2 is now the default.

## Gaps
- I didn't read the full migration guide.
- I didn't check MySQL or SQLite changes, or look for breaking changes beyond the three listed.
- I didn't run `last30days`, so there's no social or community sweep (Reddit, HN, X).
- I didn't inspect your project, so I can't say which of these affect you. If you want, I can check your `package.json`, schema and queries against the list above.

**Coverage:** vault (no prior pages), Exa (official docs, GitHub issues, blog), Tavily (dated breadth, same results), Exa fetch (docs and #5120). Not searched: Firecrawl developer index, `last30days`. No paid spend.

graders.name: answer
graders.evidence:
**Short answer:** Drizzle v1 is usable in production, but not if you apply auto-generated migrations without reading them. Details are on the vault page [[Drizzle ORM v1]].

**What breaks from 0.x** (official upgrade guide, [orm.drizzle.team/docs/upgrade-v1](https://orm.drizzle.team/docs/upgrade-v1), v1.0 released 2026-09-15):
- **Relational queries v2** is now the default.
- **`drizzle-kit push`** is renamed to **`drizzle-kit sync`**. Update any scripts and CI that call it.
- **PostgreSQL drivers** must be node-postgres 9+ or postgres.js 4+.

The same page has a step-by-step migration guide. I read only the summary of it, so I haven't checked the individual steps.
